### Observed differences

- In the earlier window, all observed outgoing transitions of activity A17 led to A40 (100% of 58 observed transitions). In the later window, A17 still led mostly to A40 — about 97 in 100 observed outgoing transitions — but a small share, about 3 in 100 (1 of 38 observed transitions), now led to A46, which was not observed as a successor of A17 before. [DIR001]
- The later-window profile rests on few observations (38 outgoing transitions versus 58 before), so the newly seen A17 → A46 transition is backed by a single observed case. The difference is unusual for random re-splits of the pooled data (empirical strength about 99.5 in 100 reference comparisons), but such strength cannot by itself separate a real change from a rare variant appearing in one window only. [DIR001]

### Inference

Support level: Insufficient evidence

The evidence is insufficient to infer a structural change in the process. Only one indicator qualified, which is the same order as the roughly 0.46 items expected by chance alone when nothing changed, and the single candidate difference (a possible new edge A17 → A46) rests on one observed transition out of 38 in the later window, so a rare variant in an otherwise unchanged process cannot be ruled out.

Let me analyse this evidence.

We have one evidence item: DIR001, a control-flow direction indicator for activity A17. Before: A17's outgoing transitions went 100% to A40. After: about 97.4% to A40 and about 2.6% to A46. So a new edge A17 → A46 appeared in the later window, small share.

Support: before 58 outgoing transitions observed, after 38 outgoing transitions observed. So the after share of 2.6% corresponds to 1 out of 38 outgoing transitions. That's very few observations — 1 transition out of 38. Weak.

Empirical strength: 0.995 — high, meaning the difference is unusual for random splits. But with only 38 outgoing transitions in the after window and 1 going to A46, this could easily be a rare variant.

Screening: 92 units tested, 0.46 items expected without change. We have 1 item. Per instructions: "A count of the same order as that expectation (for example one or two items when fewer than one is expected) is what an unchanged process typically produces: choose 'Insufficient evidence', however large or unusual a single item looks."

So with 1 item when 0.46 expected, that's the same order — one item when fewer than one is expected. Therefore: Insufficient evidence.
